summary:
I've been building a career assistant for phillipsben.com — a "Talk to Virtual Me" bot that fields questions about my work using only what's published on the site. No vector database: the knowledge pack (~12k tokens) gets stuffed directly into context. The interesting constraint was keeping confidential details out structurally, not just instructionally — a build-time redaction guard assembles the pack before the model ever sees it, so there's nothing to leak. It passed a 16/16 adversarial battery on Claude Haiku: fabrication probes, prompt injection, off-topic deflection. Backend is pluggable; I benchmarked local inference on a Pascal-era P100 (~10s warm, ~48s cold prefill on the 11k pack) and chose Haiku as the default on latency, keeping the local stack as an opt-in.

The site's project pages each get a generated hero image. ComfyUI runs on that same P100, and I've built out a pipeline: generate an abstract editorial SDXL render, then duotone it to the site palette and drop it as a webp. The generative work turned out to be as much prompt engineering as anything else — literal nouns cue the wrong geometry (columns became architecture, "message bus" became a literal coach bus), and line-centric prompts drifted into diagonal curves. Dot-field and stipple prompts are far more reliable on this checkpoint. I've generated heroes for about a dozen projects now, the most stubborn of which took four or five seeds and a rewritten prompt to land.

Hermes, the agent that refreshes the phillipsben.com dashboard daily, runs its primary model as a local Gemma 4 26B on the P100 via a llama.cpp server I built and wired into a priority-aware proxy. Getting the dashboard cron stable took some work: a DRY repetition-penalty sampler corrupted repeated identifiers in tool calls (paths, filenames, the repo name), so the model kept mangling its own shell commands. Disabling DRY was necessary but not sufficient — the Q4 quantization still struggled with exact long paths in agentic runs, so I re-architected the refresh to keep exact filesystem paths out of the model's hands entirely. A deterministic shell script handles the plumbing; the model writes short prose artifacts and calls two commands.

On the hardware side, I traced a 30-minute hang in a Hermes voice session to a missing `--n-predict` cap on the llama.cpp server — no output ceiling meant a repetition loop generated 53,000 tokens over half an hour, holding the single P100 slot and queuing every follow-up. A 4096-token hard cap bounds the worst case to about two and a half minutes. I also found that the workstation's RAM had been running at DDR4-2133 (JEDEC default) instead of the kit's rated 3600 — flipping the DOCP profile in the BIOS lifted the model's decode speed by about 18%, which matters because the 26B slightly overflows the 16GB P100 and runs partly off system RAM.

highlights.oneLiner: Bounded career assistant live on phillipsben.com — context-stuffed, adversarially tested 16/16
Generating duotoned SDXL heroes for project pages; dot/stipple prompts proved most reliable
Stabilizing the daily dashboard cron on local Gemma 4 26B — re-architected to keep exact paths out of model tool calls
Site infrastructure: hero pipeline, assistant band, and dashboard refresh all landing on main
